title: Underage Drinking: A National Concern

jokes.text: Even Sweet Dee's getting lucky! / That dude's gonna bang your sister, bro.
jokes.setup: Everyone is celebrating what a great night it is at Paddy's, with beautiful people everywhere
jokes.punchline: The 'win' for Dee is immediately undercut — her brother's friend casually announces a guy is going to sleep with his own sister, with zero filter or concern
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open joke that immediately establishes the show's moral universe. The warmth of 'Even Sweet Dee's getting lucky!' sets up a brief moment of goodwill toward Dee, then it's obliterated by Mac/Dennis's total indifference to the fact that someone is about to sleep with their sister/friend. The economy is excellent — it's one sentence and it tells you everything about these characters. High quotability and sets up a running gag.

jokes.text: Charlie dancing euphorically while Mac and Dennis watch approvingly — 'I love that little man.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are hyped about the great crowd at Paddy's
jokes.punchline: Charlie, apparently already drunk, is dancing ecstatically and Mac responds with sincere affection like a parent watching a child — 'I love that little man'
jokes.explanation: Works because Mac's paternal affection for Charlie is perfectly in character — it's a sweet moment in the middle of chaos, made funny by the condescension implicit in 'that little man.' Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis slowly realizing the crowd is very, very young — 'Kind of a young crowd, right?' 'Yeah. Really, really young.'
jokes.setup: They've been celebrating what a great night it is with so many 'beautiful people'
jokes.punchline: The dawning realization that all these beautiful people are teenagers, delivered with exquisite slow-burn understatement
jokes.explanation: The gradual escalation — 'kind of young' to 'really, really young' — is well-structured. The rewatch bonus is high because on rewatches you appreciate how the whole cold open was showing them ogling what are now obviously children. The beat earns its laugh through structure rather than a single killer line.

jokes.text: 'Everybody, out!'
jokes.setup: The uncertain 'Twenty-one?' has just confirmed the entire bar is underage
jokes.punchline: Dennis's instant, flat, no-hesitation 'Everybody, out!' — no processing, no moral deliberation, pure liability response
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the opening sequence. Two words, perfectly timed. The joke is entirely in the economy and immediacy — there's no moral hand-wringing, just a flat managerial response. Works as a great act-break button.

jokes.text: Mac solemnly declares 'And we also have a social responsibility to keep teenagers from drinking.'
jokes.setup: The gang is debating blame for letting minors in; Dennis is trying to appeal to their responsibility
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers a sincere-sounding civic statement — which we know will immediately be abandoned the moment it becomes inconvenient
jokes.explanation: The joke is ironic foreshadowing — Mac is about to spend the entire episode doing the opposite. Works better on rewatch when you know the full arc. In the moment it's a mild setup beat.

jokes.text: 'We would almost get raped and/or murdered and/or stabbed by crackheads in Fairmount Park.'
jokes.setup: Mac is making a compassionate argument that they should let underage kids drink at Paddy's because when they were young they'd get kicked out of bars and drink in parks
jokes.punchline: His memory of what happened in the park is 'almost getting raped and/or murdered and/or stabbed by crackheads' — delivered as a neutral data point in his argument that the bar is safer
jokes.explanation: This is where the episode hits its first real peak. The tripling of horrors ('raped AND/OR murdered AND/OR stabbed') with the 'and/or' legal phrasing is inspired — it makes the violence sound like a liability checklist. And it's deployed as a POSITIVE argument for why Paddy's is better. The character integration is excellent: Mac is genuinely trying to be helpful while describing childhood trauma. 'By crackheads in Fairmount Park' is a perfect specificity button.

jokes.text: 'We drove Nicky Potnik's car into a tree on Kelly Drive. With Sweet Dee in the backseat puking because some guy talked to her that she liked, remember?'
jokes.setup: Mac continues his argument about the dangers of underage drinking in parks, citing more personal history
jokes.punchline: Dee's specific humiliation — she gets so nervous when a guy she likes talks to her that she drinks herself sick and then pukes in a car that crashes — delivered as casual shared memory
jokes.explanation: This is great character work — it establishes Dee's humiliating history while simultaneously being a callback mechanism for her storyline in this episode. The specificity of 'Nicky Potnik's car' and 'Kelly Drive' gives it an authentic Philly texture. The punchline about Dee getting drunk when a guy she likes talks to her is a perfect character reveal that pays off in her subplot.

jokes.text: Mac recounts Dee's pattern: 'Every time some guy talks to you that you like, you get so nervous you drink yourself into oblivion.' Dee: 'I had bad potato salad.'
jokes.setup: Mac is describing Dee's anxiety-drinking pattern as evidence of alcohol's dangers for young people
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat denial — 'I had bad potato salad' — is the most transparent, feeble lie imaginable, and she delivers it with dead seriousness
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent line. 'I had bad potato salad' is the kind of denial so specific and so implausible that it loops back around to being hilarious. The economy is impeccable — four words that tell you everything about Dee's self-delusion. High quotability. This is the kind of line that becomes a fan favorite.

jokes.text: Mac reframes serving minors as fulfilling 'a social responsibility' to provide a safe haven — repeating Dennis's exact phrase from earlier but inverting its meaning
jokes.setup: Dennis earlier appealed to their 'social responsibility' to NOT serve minors
jokes.punchline: Mac co-opts the exact phrase to argue they have 'a social responsibility' to serve minors — using the same language to justify the opposite conclusion
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — Mac uses Dennis's own moral language to reach the opposite moral conclusion. It's a callback that doubles as character comedy: Mac has absolutely no actual principles, just a desire to seem principled while doing what he wants.

jokes.text: 'Listen, we water down the drinks, jack up the prices. We could make a serious profit off these kids. And they'd have no idea what the hell's going on. We would actually be doing something good.'
jokes.setup: The gang is debating setting up 'ground rules' to protect minors at Paddy's
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'good deed' turns out to be a price-gouging scheme to defraud teenagers — and he genuinely believes 'we would actually be doing something good'
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny moral inversion — the 'good deed' is exploitation. What makes it work is Mac's total sincerity: 'We would actually be doing something good.' He has genuinely convinced himself. This is the thesis statement of the episode's central joke, and it's executed well.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I don't know how you guys live with yourselves.' Mac/Charlie (simultaneously): 'One day at a time.' 'One day at a time.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is expressing moral disgust at the scheme to profit off teenagers
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's synchronized, completely unfazed response — 'One day at a time' — delivered like a recovery slogan, suggesting they've made peace with their own awfulness
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The synchronized delivery of a 12-step recovery cliché as a response to 'how do you live with yourselves?' is genuinely inspired — it implies they've needed to develop coping mechanisms for their own depravity. The economy is exceptional (four words total), the character integration is perfect (both Mac and Charlie are equally unbothered), and it's profoundly quotable. This earns its 8+ rating.

jokes.text: Dennis talking on the phone: 'Yeah, I know, Mom. I heard you the first time... I'm perfectly aware of what time it is... Yeah, I know how old I am. Did you think that I forgot, maybe, how old...'
jokes.setup: Cold cut to Dennis apparently living at home, taking an irritated phone call
jokes.punchline: His mom is calling to remind him of his age — the specificity of 'Did you think that I forgot how old I am?' suggests she's making a pointed comment about him still living there / being immature, and he's deeply defensive
jokes.explanation: Good scene-setting character moment. The implication that Dennis's mom is calling to point out he's too old for whatever he's doing (hanging out with high schoolers, essentially) is ironic given the episode's themes. Works as cringe but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dennis tells his mom he has 'a date this afternoon with my friend Steven' — the name and framing sounds like he's talking about a playdate
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to get off the phone with his mom, citing a social engagement
jokes.punchline: 'A date this afternoon with my friend Steven' sounds like something a child says, not a grown man — reinforcing that Dennis is fundamentally adolescent
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — the infantile framing is the gag, but it's not punched very hard. Functions more as atmosphere and character establishment than a strong individual joke.

jokes.text: Dee answers a call from 'Trey from last night' and immediately says 'I don't think I should be talking with you' before he tells her she's the most beautiful woman he's ever met
jokes.setup: Dee answers and seems to have moral reservations about talking to this person
jokes.punchline: The moment he flatters her, all reservations evaporate instantly — her 'I shouldn't be talking to you' lasts approximately three seconds
jokes.explanation: Clean character joke about Dee's desperate need for validation overriding any moral compass. The structure is tight — moral statement followed immediately by its abandonment. Well-executed.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Lemon Hill? That's where all the cool kids used to go.' Trey: 'Good. So you've been there.' Dee: 'Oh! Come on. I've been there, like, 200 times.'
jokes.setup: Trey invites Dee to Lemon Hill and she immediately reveals she knows it as a 'cool kids' spot — tipping her hand that she wasn't cool
jokes.punchline: Her over-defensive 'I've been there like 200 times' is a classic protesting-too-much move from someone who was definitely not cool enough to go to Lemon Hill
jokes.explanation: Solid if unremarkable joke about Dee's high school insecurity. The '200 times' overclaim is a good specific number. Character-consistent.

jokes.text: Trey watches Dee shotgun a beer or chug aggressively: 'Wow. You can really put 'em back, can't you?' Dee: 'The trick is to just kind of open your throat.'
jokes.setup: Dee is hanging out with Trey's high school friends at Lemon Hill, trying to fit in
jokes.punchline: She's apparently drinking so aggressively that a high schooler is impressed, and her response is to give a clinical technique — she's so practiced at anxiety-drinking she has actual tips
jokes.explanation: Pays off the established joke about Dee's anxiety-drinking. 'The trick is to just kind of open your throat' is a great specific line that reveals this isn't a one-off — she has technique. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: 'Of course they are. They haven't realized how much life sucks yet.'
jokes.setup: Mac comments on how much fun the high schoolers are having at Paddy's
jokes.punchline: Dennis's flat, nihilistic explanation: they're having fun because they don't yet know life is terrible
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan line. The nihilism is authentic to Dennis's character and it's delivered with just the right amount of casualness. 'They haven't realized how much life sucks yet' has the economy and darkness that characterizes the show at its best.

jokes.text: Mac: 'High school was the best.' Dennis: 'Do you guys even remember high school? I don't think it happened the way you think.' Mac: 'The only reason you got to hang out with me and the other cool kids is 'cause you sold us all weed. Everybody thought you were an asshole.' Mac: 'I was popular!'
jokes.setup: Mac is nostalgically reminiscing about how great high school was
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals Mac was only 'popular' because he was the drug dealer — and Mac's delusional insistence that he was genuinely popular
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. Mac's self-delusion about his high school popularity is a perfect window into his character — he fundamentally believes he was cool. 'Everybody thought you were an asshole' delivered as plain fact is excellent. Mac's indignant 'I was popular!' closes it perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Mac was very popular. And I like to think I was pretty popular myself.' 'No, he was. You were popular like a clown is popular.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to co-sign Mac's popularity claim while sneaking in his own
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects the record: Charlie was 'popular like a clown is popular' — people found him entertaining but not someone you'd respect or take seriously
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest lines in the episode. 'Popular like a clown is popular' is a legitimately great insult — it's specific, it's devastating, it perfectly defines Charlie's social role, and it has genuine wit rather than just being mean. The setup (Charlie trying to include himself in the popularity claim) makes the punchline land harder. Genuinely quotable. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, you made us all laugh. All the guys knew you couldn't sleep with their girlfriends.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining what 'popular like a clown' means for Charlie
jokes.punchline: The clarification that Charlie was unthreatening to the point where his sexual impotence (socially) was a known, accepted fact among the friend group
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke — 'everyone knew you couldn't sleep with their girlfriends' is a specific and cruel elaboration on the clown metaphor. Well-integrated.

jokes.text: Charlie retaliates: 'Whatever, dude. The only reason you got laid is 'cause you dated freshmen. Yeah. You've always had that creepy thing with younger girls.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is wounded by the clown comparison and fires back at Dennis
jokes.punchline: He reveals Dennis has 'always had that creepy thing with younger girls' — which is both a great insult AND the central joke of the episode's Dennis subplot (he's about to be hit on by an 18-year-old)
jokes.explanation: Smart piece of setup work — Charlie's accusation that Dennis has 'that creepy thing with younger girls' ironically foreshadows the Dennis subplot where he's pursued by an 18-year-old. Character integration is strong. Rewatch bonus for the ironic payoff.

jokes.text: Mac's defense: 'You guys sniffing glue in your mom's basement. That's creepy.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is trading insults about each other's high school weirdness
jokes.punchline: Mac casually reveals that Charlie (and apparently Mac) used to huff glue — framed as a defensive counter-attack but actually just confirming another humiliating detail
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the later glue-sniffing scene. The reveal that Mac/Charlie were basement glue-sniffers is both a good insult AND seeds the later scene where they actually try to sniff glue. Rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Mac reveals: 'Tim Murphy slept with your prom date.' Dennis denies. Mac escalates: 'Tim Murphy slept with your prom date!' Charlie piles on: 'Tim Murphy had sex with your prom date!'
jokes.setup: Mac has a devastating fact about Dennis's high school humiliation
jokes.punchline: The triple repetition with escalating formality ('slept with' → 'had sex with') as Dennis progressively breaks down — and Charlie adding the clinical restatement for maximum damage
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. The genius is that Charlie's 'Tim Murphy had sex with your prom date!' adds nothing new — it's the exact same information — but the more clinical phrasing and the pile-on nature makes it land harder. Mac's flat 'That's right.' seals it. The structure of three characters beating the same drum until Dennis breaks is classic sitcom escalation done well.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie watching Dennis react: 'Oh. He's getting sad now.' 'Now he's running away.' 'Oh, is he gonna cry?' 'Did you see that? He was totally gonna cry.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been told (repeatedly) that Tim Murphy slept with his prom date
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie narrate Dennis's visible emotional collapse in real time, like sports commentators calling a breakdown — including the implied visual of Dennis actually fleeing
jokes.explanation: The commentary format — 'he's getting sad,' 'now he's running away,' 'is he gonna cry?' — is a great comedic choice. It treats Dennis's genuine emotional pain as entertainment, which is very on-brand. The narration adds to the humiliation.

jokes.text: Dee and Trey are about to kiss. Trey pulls back: 'Wait! I can't do this.' Dee: 'What?' Trey: 'I never statutory raped anyone before.'
jokes.setup: Trey and Dee are having a romantic moment; Trey pulls back as if having a sudden moral crisis
jokes.punchline: His moral crisis is not 'she's too old for me' but 'I've never statutory raped anyone' — framing the crime from his (the minor's) perspective about committing statutory rape on the adult
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever inversion. The legal/moral framing of 'statutory rape' is applied from the wrong direction — the teenager is framing himself as the potential perpetrator, which is both legally confused and darkly funny. It subverts the expected 'I shouldn't be doing this' beat. The originality is real: flipping which party 'commits' statutory rape is a sharp comedic concept. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dee's response to 'I never statutory raped anyone before': 'Let's, uh, just take it slow.' Trey: 'You are so sweet. Where were you when I was in high school?' Dee: 'I was eight.'
jokes.setup: Trey asks romantically 'Where were you when I was in high school?'
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat, matter-of-fact 'I was eight' — the math of the age gap delivered as a romance-killing fact
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. 'I was eight' is as economical as comedy gets — it simultaneously answers the romantic question literally, destroys the romantic mood, and mathematically confirms the inappropriateness of the situation. The flatness of delivery makes it land harder. One of the most quotable lines in the episode. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Mac claims he's cutting kids off after 3 drinks: 'Plus, there's so much water, they're probably more hydrated than they ever have been.'
jokes.setup: Charlie observes the kids are wasted despite Mac claiming to have cut them off
jokes.punchline: Mac's justification — framing watered-down drinks as a health benefit ('more hydrated than they ever have been') — is a perfect specimen of his self-serving logic
jokes.explanation: Very good character comedy. Mac turning the watered-down drink scheme into a health argument is exactly his brand of motivated reasoning. 'More hydrated than they ever have been' is a great specific phrase.

jokes.text: Mac breaks up a teenage couple's fight, plays tough mediator, gets praised by Sara: 'Charlie, that was the coolest thing you've ever done!' Charlie: 'I know. I'm gonna be sick.'
jokes.setup: Mac plays cool authority figure breaking up a teenage fight, and Sara praises 'Charlie' (a mix-up or misdirection) for being cool
jokes.punchline: Charlie accepts the praise, then immediately undercuts any cool by announcing he's going to be sick — the adrenaline/alcohol getting to him
jokes.explanation: Good self-deflating joke. Charlie (or Mac) accepts cool-guy praise and then immediately reveals his body is betraying him. The beat-perfect timing of 'I know. I'm gonna be sick.' subverts the cool moment.

jokes.text: An 18-year-old girl approaches Dennis: 'You Dennis Reynolds? You like what you see?' Dennis: 'Uh, I don't know.' Girl: 'Dude, relax. I'm 18.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been lecturing everyone about not getting involved with minors
jokes.punchline: He's immediately hit on by an 18-year-old who reads his hesitation and reassures him she's legal — reversing the dynamic completely
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the Dennis subplot setup. The girl proactively volunteering her age ('Dude, relax, I'm 18') as if she's dealt with this before is a sharp detail. The irony of Dennis being pursued despite his stated principles is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Doesn't seem to bother your sister. She was all over this one boy in my class today.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just told an 18-year-old high schooler to get lost because she's in high school.
jokes.punchline: She reveals his sister Dee is currently hanging out with a boy in her class — confirming Dee has sunk lower than Dennis's already-low bar.
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — the worlds collide and Dennis learns his sister is doing what he just refused to do. Efficiently delivered with just enough cringe.

jokes.text: Dennis asks 'Are you in high school?' She says yes. 'Then take a hike.' She: 'Doesn't seem to bother your sister.'
jokes.setup: Dennis turns the girl down because she's in high school even though she's 18
jokes.punchline: She fires back that it doesn't bother his sister — meaning Dee is currently with a high school guy
jokes.explanation: Smart callback that links the two sibling storylines. Dennis's principled refusal is immediately undercut by the girl's knowledge of his sister's hypocrisy. Good economy.

jokes.text: The girl gives Dennis her number and says 'if you're looking for the ride of your life, give me a call.' Dennis: 'Goddamn it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just turned down the girl on principle
jokes.punchline: 'Goddamn it' — the flat, resigned frustration of a man fighting his own desires — implies he's going to call
jokes.explanation: Decent button joke. 'Goddamn it' as a reaction to being attracted to someone you've decided not to pursue is relatable and character-appropriate. Economy is good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dennis confronts Dee about hanging out with a high school kid. Dee: 'We're just friends. He went through a really bad breakup, and he just needed me to be there for him.' Dennis: 'What you're doing is sick and wrong.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is accusing Dee of something inappropriate
jokes.punchline: Dee's earnest 'he just needed me to be there for him' is an exact replica of what anyone would say about a friend — except the friend is a teenager she's romantically involved with
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. Dee's earnest defense is well-pitched but the joke is fairly predictable at this point.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Are you living out some sad fantasy of yours? Going out with the most popular kid in high school.' Dee: 'Why would that be a fantasy? I went out with tons of guys in high school.' Dennis: 'You wore that scoliosis back brace until you were 20 years old. Everyone was afraid of you. You looked like a monster!'
jokes.setup: Dee claims she dated plenty in high school and doesn't have unfulfilled fantasies
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the definitive account of Dee's high school reality — the scoliosis brace, being 20, everyone being afraid of her, 'you looked like a monster'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dee-destruction jokes in the episode. The scoliosis brace detail is both specific and devastating, and 'you looked like a monster' is delivered with such casual certainty that it's perfect. The character integration is exceptional — this speaks to Dee's core wound, which explains all her behavior in this episode. The payoff of the earlier back brace mention earns a rewatch bonus. Genuinely earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie trying to sniff glue: 'I'm telling you, this is the wrong kind of glue, Charlie.' 'No, it's not.' 'This is made for, like, kindergartners or something.' 'No, this will work.' 'No, look. Nontoxic and safe.' 'We don't want safe. We want toxic.'
jokes.setup: Mac mentioned they used to sniff glue; now we see them actually attempting it in real time
jokes.punchline: They've bought the wrong kind of glue (non-toxic, safe, 'for kindergartners'), and the debate over its suitability — 'we don't want safe, we want toxic' — is delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedic payoff. 'We don't want safe. We want toxic.' is the best line in the episode — it's the most concentrated expression of the gang's essential philosophy. The callback from Mac's earlier accusation landing here as a fully realized scene is great structure. The kindergartner glue detail is perfect specificity. The character integration is as good as it gets for these two. This line is genuinely quotable and captures the show's ethos. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie arrive at Sara's high school party. Mac: 'Kind of a lame party, bro.' Charlie: 'Uh, what do you think? Should we jet?' Mac: 'Yeah. This doesn't feel right.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie crashed a high school party, ostensibly out of concern for the kids
jokes.punchline: Their primary complaint is that the party is 'lame' and doesn't feel right — not because they're adults at a teenage party, but because the party quality is insufficient
jokes.explanation: Good ironic character moment — their discomfort at the party is about the vibe, not any moral dimension. 'This doesn't feel right' said for entirely the wrong reasons is on-brand.

jokes.text: Sara asks Mac and Charlie to get the keg since her brother bailed. They hemm and haw about it being 'one thing at the bar where we have control over you guys' — then Sara says 'you've been so cool' and 'this would be the coolest thing anyone's ever done for us' and they cave instantly.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are posturing as responsible adults who can't provide alcohol to minors
jokes.punchline: Two compliments from a teenage girl completely dissolve their principles — 'the coolest thing anyone's ever done for us' triggers immediate capitulation
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The speed at which 'we can't do this' becomes 'who wants to do a keg stand?' when teenagers call them cool is a perfect expression of Mac and Charlie's arrested development. The 'coolest thing anyone's ever done for us' line doing such heavy lifting is funny.

jokes.text: 'Who wants to do a keg stand?!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have been going back and forth about whether they should provide alcohol to minors
jokes.punchline: The 180-degree turn is so complete that Mac isn't just getting the keg — he's actively organizing the keg stand, transforming from reluctant adult to enthusiastic party host
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The jump from 'I don't think that's a good idea' to 'Who wants to do a keg stand?!' is so dramatic that the economy of the single exclamatory line does all the work needed.

jokes.text: Dee expresses second thoughts about being at the high school party. Trey: 'Oh, come on. It'll be a blast.' Dee: 'Yeah, well, I don't think your friends like me that much.'
jokes.setup: Dee has arrived at a high school party as a grown adult woman
jokes.punchline: Her concern is not 'I am an adult at a teenager's party' but rather the high school social anxiety of 'your friends don't like me' — she's regressed completely
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke. The specificity of Dee's regression — she's not thinking like an adult, she's thinking like a nervous high schooler at a new party — is well-observed.

jokes.text: Mac doing a keg stand while teens count — '25, 26, 27, 28, 29!' — the visual of a 28-year-old competing at a teenage party.
jokes.setup: Mac has claimed the responsible adult role and arrived at a teenage house party.
jokes.punchline: He's upside down on a keg being counted by teenagers, completely in his element — there is no self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The visual is the joke — a nearly 30-year-old man competing at a keg stand against teenagers, with complete investment. Mostly funny as a sight gag inferred from the transcript. The numbers counting upward function as comedic escalation.

jokes.text: Mac does a keg stand and hits 77 seconds: '77 seconds! That is a new record, baby!'
jokes.setup: Mac has been doing a keg stand at the high school party
jokes.punchline: He celebrates a keg stand world record at a high school party with the unbridled triumph of someone who has achieved genuine greatness — a 30-something man extremely proud of outdrinking teenagers
jokes.explanation: Good visual/character comedy. Mac's triumph at the keg stand record is funny because of the gap between how big a deal he thinks this is and what it actually means. The specificity of '77 seconds' adds to it.

jokes.text: Dee is gossipping with teenage girls about Ben, Sara, Rachel, Caitlin, and Trey's social drama, completely absorbed in it.
jokes.setup: Dee is at a high school party
jokes.punchline: She's not maintaining adult distance — she is fully, enthusiastically engaged in high school gossip drama, saying 'Oh my God!' like a 16-year-old
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe moment. Dee being fully absorbed in teenage gossip is character-consistent and mildly funny, but it's the least surprising thing about her at this point in the episode.

jokes.text: So, Ben is, like, 'I don't care what Kevin said, Sara. I was only going out with Rachel to get closer to you.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just triumphantly landed a keg stand record.
jokes.punchline: The immediate cut to Dee and Sara gossiping about high school relationship drama — multiple new characters (Ben, Kevin, Rachel) introduced in one breath — highlights how completely Dee has regressed into a teenager.
jokes.explanation: The cringe here is Dee completely absorbed in teenage drama. The names Ben, Kevin, Rachel, Caitlin pile up absurdly. Funny as a character beat — Dee has fully regressed.

jokes.text: Dennis shows up at the party and immediately beats the keg stand record, then trash-talks the teenagers: 'Yeah! What do you think about that, bitches! Load 'em up, losers!' High schoolers: 'What's with this guy?' 'What is he, like, 40?'
jokes.setup: Dennis has presumably arrived after his principled stance at Paddy's
jokes.punchline: He's not here as a responsible adult — he's doing keg stands and trash-talking teenagers, while the teenagers look at him like he's a pathetic old man
jokes.explanation: Very good ironic character payoff. Dennis abandoned his principles so thoroughly that he's now trash-talking teenagers at a keg stand. 'What is he, like, 40?' from the teens is the perfect external perspective on the gang's arrested development. High impact.

jokes.text: Dee announces: 'Trey asked me to prom last night. This is getting really weird.' Mac: 'That girl Sara asked me too.' Dennis: 'What? No, we can't go to the prom. That's pathetic. What do you mean 'we'? Who asked you?'
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to leave the party
jokes.punchline: Multiple members of the gang have been asked to prom by teenagers — and Dennis's indignant 'we can't go, that's pathetic' immediately switches to 'who asked YOU?' when he realizes he wasn't invited
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating reveal structure. Each new prom invitation is a comedic escalation, but the best part is Dennis's hypocrisy — he goes from 'that's pathetic, we can't go' to immediate injured pride at not being asked, all in the same breath. 'What do you mean 'we'? Who asked you?' is the perfect hypocritical pivot.

jokes.text: That girl Sara asked me too. / You're kidding! / What? No, we can't go to the prom. That's pathetic. / What do you mean 'we'? Who asked you?
jokes.setup: Dee reveals she was asked to prom. Charlie also reveals Sara asked him.
jokes.punchline: Mac's immediate 'What do you mean "we"? Who asked you?' — revealing Mac was not asked to prom and is therefore excluded.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural beat. The 'Who asked you?' realization that Mac alone was excluded from the prom invites sets up the rest of the episode's Mac subplot beautifully. Good economy — makes the beat clear in four words.

jokes.text: An 18-year-old girl shows up at Dennis's door wanting him to take her to prom — and threatens to report the bar to police if he doesn't.
jokes.setup: Dennis turned this girl down at the bar; now she's at his apartment
jokes.punchline: The 'ride of your life' girl is now blackmailing him — the flirtation has turned into extortion, and she's completely calm about it
jokes.explanation: Good dark escalation. Taking the flirtatious encounter and turning it into blackmail is a sharp plot twist that fits the show's tone. The girl being totally matter-of-fact about the extortion is well-played.

jokes.text: Mac announces 'I don't think we should be serving minors anymore.' Dennis: 'Oh, no. Somebody's jealous.' Mac: 'I'm not jealous. I just think it's dangerous.' Dennis: 'You're jealous you didn't get asked to the prom.'
jokes.setup: Mac seems to have had a change of heart about the underage drinking scheme
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately diagnoses the real reason: Mac wasn't asked to prom and he's jealous — his sudden morality is wounded pride
jokes.explanation: Good ironic reversal — Mac's moral stance is transparently about not being invited. Dennis calling it immediately is sharp. The joke that none of them have real principles, only wounded egos, is well-expressed here.

jokes.text: They all slowly reveal they've each been asked to prom, then proceed to agree to go one by one. Mac: 'So all of you guys got asked to the prom?' Dennis: 'Oh, this is so lame!' — then immediately: 'At least you don't actually have to go.' Mac: 'Are you going?' Dennis: 'Yeah. I have to.' Mac: 'Oh well, if you're going, I'm going then, I guess.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is trying to claim they're not going to the prom
jokes.punchline: One by one they all capitulate — 'I have to,' 'if you're going I'm going,' 'I didn't get to go in high school so it might be fun' — a cascade of rationalized surrender
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy. The cascading agreement to go to prom — each person using the previous person's capitulation as cover — is well-constructed. The logic that 'I have to' (blackmail) triggers everyone else to decide they want to go is a perfect expression of the gang's collective self-deception.

jokes.text: Charlie argues that someone should have invited Mac: 'Maybe if you weren't such a jerk, someone might have asked you. Because Sara told me that Maureen told her that Regina McGinley thought you were cute.'
jokes.setup: Mac is upset he wasn't asked to prom
jokes.punchline: Charlie's attempt to console Mac via second-hand high school gossip chain ('Sara told me that Maureen told her that Regina McGinley thought you were cute') is both sweet and completely pathetic from a grown man
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. The specificity of the gossip chain ('Sara told Maureen told her that Regina McGinley...') is funny because it's so authentically high school — Charlie has been gossipping with teenagers and absorbed their social intelligence. Mac's reaction to this information will presumably be pathetic.

jokes.text: Maybe if you weren't such a jerk, someone might have asked you. Because Sara told me that Maureen told her that Regina McGinley thought you were cute.
jokes.setup: Mac is calling everyone pathetic for going to prom.
jokes.punchline: Charlie tries to soften the blow by relaying a chain of hearsay compliments ('Sara told me that Maureen told her that Regina McGinley thought you were cute') — which is both consoling and completely trivializing.
jokes.explanation: The chain of gossip relay — 'Sara told me that Maureen told her' — perfectly captures how Charlie processes social information through a teenage lens. High character integration for Charlie, who apparently has become fully embedded in high school social networks.

jokes.text: Charlie starts rambling about 'Ray Rafferty comes up to you at the party and you're...' and Mac shuts him down: 'Charlie, shut up!' Dennis: 'The only reason Sara asked you in the first place is because you're the only idiot dumb enough to listen to her bitch about her ex-boyfriend all night!'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to relay high school gossip about Mac's potential admirer
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts through it all: Sara only asked Charlie because he was willing to listen to her complain about her ex — his prom invitation was a utility, not attraction
jokes.explanation: Sharp Dennis moment. The reveal that Charlie's prom invite was purely transactional (he listened to her ex drama) is both a callback and a devastating put-down. 'The only idiot dumb enough to listen to her bitch about her ex-boyfriend all night' is a great specific insult.

jokes.text: Then Ray Rafferty comes up to you at the party and you're... / Charlie, shut up!
jokes.setup: Charlie is continuing to relay a chain of high school social information.
jokes.punchline: Mac shuts him down before he can finish — implying the story would be worse for Mac. The 'shut up!' after a moment of near-exposure is a classic running gag button.
jokes.explanation: The cut-off works as a beat and implies something worse was coming, which is funnier than whatever the actual story would be.

jokes.text: Dee comes out in her old high school dress. Dennis: 'Wow. You look... You look... Yeah.' Dee: 'I know. I feel so lucky this thing even fits still.' Dennis: 'Is that your dress from high school?' Dee: 'Yup.' Dennis: 'You didn't go to the prom in high school, Dee.' Dee: 'No, I know.'
jokes.setup: Dee emerges in a dress she's apparently kept for decades
jokes.punchline: Dennis can't even finish a compliment ('You look... Yeah.'), and the reveal that she kept a prom dress she never wore to prom is quietly devastating
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest moments in the episode. Dennis's inability to finish 'You look...' is perfect — the ellipses do the work. 'You didn't go to the prom in high school, Dee.' 'No, I know.' is an exchange of such specific, quiet sadness that it's funny and genuinely touching. The character integration is exceptional — this is Dee's whole arc crystallized. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Oh, Dee! Come here. Let me take a look at you. / Wow. You look... You look... Yeah. / I know. I feel so lucky that this thing even fits still.
jokes.setup: Dee emerges in her prom dress before the prom. Dennis's reaction is meant to be evaluative.
jokes.punchline: His complete inability to find something complimentary to say — trailing off into 'Yeah' — which Dee misreads as stunned appreciation.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's trailing 'Yeah' as the only honest reaction he can muster, while Dee takes it as a compliment, is excellent cringe comedy. The comedic pause-work here is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Dee: 'My back brace was under the dress, and Mom called me fat. So I stayed home and cried instead.'
jokes.setup: We just learned Dee has kept a prom dress she never wore
jokes.punchline: The full story: she had the dress, the brace was under it, her mom called her fat — a trifecta of teenage tragedy delivered in a single sentence with no self-pity, just flat recitation
jokes.explanation: The best Dee joke in the episode and one of the best in the season. The accumulation of humiliations — brace, fat-shaming mom, staying home to cry — delivered in a single matter-of-fact sentence is devastating comedy. The absence of self-pity is what makes it work: she just states it as historical record. The economy is near-perfect. The character integration is exceptional — this is the most concentrated version of Dee's whole character. Earns the 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Mac crashes into the prom scene: 'What's up, bitches? Mmm! You assholes aren't gonna be the only ones having fun. I'm going to the prom.' Dennis: 'Dork! You cannot crash a high school prom.' Mac: 'I'm going stag, bro.'
jokes.setup: Everyone else has a prom date; Mac was excluded
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution to not being invited is to 'go stag' — to a high school prom he wasn't invited to, as a grown man, with absolute confidence
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke. 'I'm going stag, bro' as a response to 'you can't crash a high school prom' is perfect Mac. His complete lack of self-awareness about the social violation is very on-brand.

jokes.text: Mac to Dee: 'Mac, you are so pathetic.' Mac: 'Yes, and your eyebrows are drawn on, so...'
jokes.setup: Dee is calling Mac pathetic for crashing the prom stag
jokes.punchline: Mac's non-sequitur comeback — 'your eyebrows are drawn on' — is a truly random personal attack that has nothing to do with the argument, and yet lands perfectly
jokes.explanation: Great non-sequitur. 'Your eyebrows are drawn on, so...' is funny because it's completely unrelated to the argument, yet specific enough to feel like a real observation. The trailing 'so...' implies it somehow negates her entire point. High quotability — this is exactly the kind of left-field insult the show does well.

jokes.text: Mac sees Dee leave with Trey: 'Trey is so cool.' Beat. 'He's totally gonna bang your sister.'
jokes.setup: Trey arrives to pick up Dee for prom
jokes.punchline: Mac returns to his opening line — 'He's totally gonna bang your sister' — completing the running gag from the cold open
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. The callback to the opening line gives the episode a satisfying structural closure. The deadpan delivery of such a crass observation as a neutral fact is very Mac.

jokes.text: Dee to Trey: 'Wow! You look... good.' Trey: 'I know! Like a princess.' Dee: 'Can I tell you a little secret?' Trey: 'Sure.' Dee: 'Beat it.'
jokes.setup: Dee is greeting her teenage prom date and starts to whisper something romantic
jokes.punchline: 'Beat it' — she's not telling Trey a secret, she's telling Mac to leave, dismissing him in the most blunt possible way mid-romantic-moment
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured misdirection joke. 'Can I tell you a little secret?' sets up an intimate romantic beat; 'Beat it' is both maximally economical and perfectly subversive. Works as both a Dee-character joke and a great structural beat.

jokes.text: Trey confides: 'I always wanted to have sex on prom.'
jokes.setup: Trey has just been introduced as Dee's sweet teenage prom date
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals his only interest in prom is having sex — delivered as an earnest, naive confession rather than a threat, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Decent dark joke. The naivety of the delivery undercuts the creepiness in a way that makes it funny. Fairly predictable for a teenage male character but executed efficiently.

jokes.text: Mac's 18-year-old prom date arrives, and Mac is immediately proud: 'She's unbelievable. How old is she?' Dennis: 'She's 18.' Mac: 'You are a lucky man.' Dennis: 'Oh, you dick!'
jokes.setup: Everyone mocked Dennis earlier for his 'creepy thing with younger girls'
jokes.punchline: Dennis has an 18-year-old date and everyone is now COMPLIMENTING him — the entire moral stance evaporates the moment an attractive girl validates it
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. The moral consistency they demanded earlier is completely abandoned when Dennis's date is attractive. 'Oh, you dick!' from Dennis captures the hypocrisy perfectly.

jokes.text: Wait a second. You guys called me creepy for liking young chicks. Eighteen's legal, bro. This isn't a morality contest. / Eighteen's not young, brother. / So you guys are giving me the go-ahead? I mean, can I...? / Go ahead.
jokes.setup: Mac is pointing out the hypocrisy of being called creepy earlier while his friends now celebrate his 18-year-old date.
jokes.punchline: The group's immediate philosophical pivot — 'Eighteen's not young, brother' and 'Go ahead' — dispensing moral permission with the ease of someone handing out coupons.
jokes.explanation: 'This isn't a morality contest' is a genuinely good line — it's the show's thesis delivered as throwaway dialogue. The 'Go ahead' dispensation of permission is casual and funny.

jokes.text: 'Wait a second. You guys called me creepy for liking young chicks.' Mac: 'Eighteen's legal, bro. This isn't a morality contest.' Dennis: 'Eighteen's not young, brother.' Mac: 'So you guys are giving me the go-ahead? I mean, can I...' Dennis/Mac: 'Go ahead.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is pointing out the hypocrisy of being accused of creepiness for liking young girls, then immediately being congratulated for the same thing
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'This isn't a morality contest' perfectly encapsulates the gang's ethics — there are no principles, only shifting situational judgments. Then their instant 'go ahead' permission is hilariously hypocritical.
jokes.explanation: 'This isn't a morality contest' is a brilliantly self-aware line from Mac — it accidentally describes the entire show's ethos. The gang's instant reversal from 'that's creepy' to 'go ahead' the moment the girl is attractive is a perfect expression of their nonexistent value system. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dennis's 18-year-old prom date can't get her dress zipped because her hair is caught. Dennis: 'All right. Just pull it.' She pulls. The pained reaction noise.
jokes.setup: Dennis's prom date is struggling with her dress zipper
jokes.punchline: The practical awkwardness of a dress-zipper-hair situation, with the implied painful yank and resulting noise — mundane physical comedy
jokes.explanation: Mild physical comedy moment. The hair-in-zipper gag is familiar and doesn't have strong character integration. It functions as a beat between stronger jokes but isn't notable on its own.

jokes.text: Tammy arrives to pick up her prom date — and it turns out to be Dennis's date, who Tammy is apparently dating or going to prom with.
jokes.setup: Dennis is taking this 18-year-old girl to prom, fully committed
jokes.punchline: His date has another prom date — Tammy, Trey's ex-girlfriend — and the web of teenage romantic drama has now ensnared Dennis completely
jokes.explanation: Decent plot twist that serves to pull all the storylines together. The escalation of Dennis being trapped in teenager drama is satisfying structurally but not a knockout comedic moment on its own.

jokes.text: Trey and Dee, Tammy and Dennis's date — they all leave together. Mac: 'Oh, man! Ah, they did it. They got what they wanted.' Dennis: 'So wait a second. They were actually using you two to make each other jealous.'
jokes.setup: It's become clear the teenagers used Dee and Dennis (and Charlie) as pawns in their own romantic drama
jokes.punchline: The adults were manipulated by high schoolers into going to prom — and the teenagers got exactly what they wanted while the gang got nothing
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the episode's central irony — the supposedly worldly adults got completely played by high schoolers. The reveal is structurally satisfying and the character humiliation is well-earned.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I always knew that they'd wind up together, 'cause they're, like, so perfect for each other.' Mac: 'Shut up, Charlie!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is processing that they were used by teenagers
jokes.punchline: Charlie responds as if he were also a high school student invested in this relationship — 'I always knew they'd end up together, they're so perfect' — with zero awareness of his own manipulation
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Charlie fully drinking the high school romance Kool-Aid while everyone else is furious is perfect. His 'they're so perfect for each other' is the response of someone who has completely lost perspective.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That dude's gonna bang your prom date, bro.' Dennis: 'Stop saying it! It's not funny!'
jokes.setup: Trey has just left with both Dee and apparently their dates
jokes.punchline: Mac returns to his running line — now directed at Dennis instead of Charlie — and Dennis breaks the fourth wall slightly by saying 'stop saying it, it's not funny' (which makes it funnier)
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the running gag, now directed at Dennis after his prom date abandons him. 'Stop saying it! It's not funny!' is a perfect meta-reaction that actually confirms it IS funny. Good running gag management — each iteration lands because the target changes.

jokes.text: Mac to Dennis: 'Hey, why are you such an asshole all the time?' Dennis: 'I'm not the asshole. You guys are the ones that just got dumped on prom night.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are bickering in the aftermath of being used by teenagers
jokes.punchline: Dennis's defense is to point out that THEY got dumped on prom night — 'you guys' implying Mac is in the same sad boat — delivered as a devastating counter rather than self-reflection
jokes.explanation: Good ironic line. 'You guys just got dumped on prom night' is a great specific humiliation — and Dennis doesn't realize it applies to him too. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Mac: 'You got dumped on prom night!' Dennis: 'You were gonna go stag.' Mac: 'Yes, I was. Absolutely.' Charlie: 'How old are you, dude?' Mac: 'I am 28 years old.' Charlie: 'You're a piece of crap!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is trying to claim the moral high ground in the prom disaster
jokes.punchline: Charlie's 'How old are you, dude?' forces Mac to announce his age — '28 years old' — which puts everything in horrifying context, earning a 'You're a piece of crap!' from Charlie (who also went to this prom)
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-closing escalation. 'I am 28 years old' as a declaration of pride in the middle of this situation is funny precisely because Mac says it with zero self-awareness, and then 'You're a piece of crap!' from Charlie — who also went to the prom — is the perfect hypocritical button. The specificity of the age and the total lack of self-reflection makes this land hard.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I'm not a piece of crap! You're a piece of crap.' Charlie: 'I have to pee.' Dennis: 'Stop it. Go pee.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are in a heated argument about who is the bigger piece of crap
jokes.punchline: Charlie completely deflates the argument with 'I have to pee' — the most mundane, childlike exit from an argument imaginable — and Dennis just says 'stop it, go pee' as if parenting
jokes.explanation: Perfect button joke. 'I have to pee' as the escape from a heated argument is so anti-climactic it's brilliant. And Dennis's 'stop it, go pee' is exactly the response of a tired parent — which is ironically what he's become to these man-children. The economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Mac's final line: 'I hate you, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has defused the argument by announcing he has to pee
jokes.punchline: 'I hate you, Charlie' — not for anything specific, just as a general existential statement, delivered flatly as the final word
jokes.explanation: Decent button. 'I hate you, Charlie' as a final non-sequitur captures the gang's dynamic well — there's always someone ending up as the target of ambient hostility. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Final title card or closing beat: 'Just like high school.'
jokes.setup: The whole episode has been about the gang reliving/recreating high school
jokes.punchline: 'Just like high school' — a perfect closing line that ties together every theme in the episode: their immaturity, their humiliations, their inability to grow up
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing line. Three words that land as the episode's thesis statement. The economy is as good as it gets, and the structural function — summarizing the entire episode's theme — earns it an 8+. 'Just like high school' confirms that nothing has changed, nothing has been learned, and the gang is exactly where they were at 15. Rewatch bonus because it makes you appreciate the whole episode differently.

tmdb_overview: After reminiscing about high school, the guys conclude that it would be a public service if they allowed teens to drink in the bar, thus providing a safe and controlled environment for teens to party. Feeling that she missed out on a lot as a teenager due to having to wear a brace for her scoliosis, Dee begins dating a high school jock.
